stem.text: Use the direct comparison test to determine whether the series \( \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \), where \( a_n = \frac{9}{n^{4} + 4} \), converges or diverges. Verify the conditions of the test.

answer_key.label: The series converges by the direct comparison test, because \( 0 < a_n < \frac{9}{n^{4}} \text{ and } p = 4 > 1 \).

worked_solution.text: The terms are positive, so the direct comparison test applies. Compare with \( \sum \frac{9}{n^{4}} \), a multiple of the p-series with \( p = 4 \).
Adding \( 4 \) to the denominator makes each term smaller, so \( 0 < \frac{9}{n^{4} + 4} < \frac{9}{n^{4}} \) for every n.
The series converges by the direct comparison test, because \( 0 < a_n < \frac{9}{n^{4}} \text{ and } p = 4 > 1 \), so \( \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \) converges.

options.label: The series converges by the nth term test, because \( \lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0 \).
options.derivation: the verdict drawn from the terms approaching 0, which no test supports

options.label: The series diverges by the direct comparison test, because \( 0 < a_n < \frac{9}{n^{4}} \text{ and } p = 4 > 1 \).
options.derivation: the p-series threshold reversed, so the comparison series with p greater than 1 read as divergent

options.label: The series converges by the direct comparison test, because \( a_n \ge \frac{9}{n^{4}} \text{ and } p = 4 > 1 \).
options.derivation: the comparison inequality written the other way round, which could only support divergence
